content: The nine-month treatment regimen for multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) was modified in some cases by replacing ethionamide with linezolid. This change was evaluated using programmatic data from South Africa, which provided information on treatment outcomes for patients treated with either ethionamide or linezolid in the nine-month regimen. The data excluded patients with extensive TB disease, severe forms of extrapulmonary TB, fluoroquinolone resistance, or prior exposure to second-line treatments. The three key medicines in Group A for second-line classification were bedaquiline, fluoroquinolones, and linezolid. In 2021, evidence reviews focused on the performance of a standardized shorter regimen where the injectable agent was replaced by bedaquiline (used for six months) in combination with levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, ethionamide, ethambutol, high-dose isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and clofazimine for four months. This could be extended to six months if the patient remained sputum smear-positive at the end of four months, followed by five months of treatment with levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, clofazimine, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide. Comparisons were made with a similar regimen where ethionamide was replaced by two months of linezolid (600 mg once daily) and with longer regimens based on the 2020 WHO recommendations. The analysis used unadjusted relative risks (RRs) and adjusted relative risks (aRRs), calculated using log-binomial generalized linear regression. Confounders were adjusted using inverse probability propensity score weighting. No convergence issues arose with the log-binomial model. When outcome rates were very low (<5 cases), only unadjusted RRs were presented. For outcomes with zero events, unadjusted risk differences (RDs) were calculated. Covariates for propensity score analysis included age, gender, baseline smear results, HIV status, prior treatment history, body mass index, smoking status, diabetes diagnosis, baseline cavitation, disease site, and presence of bilateral disease. The shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen showed similar effectiveness across subgroups, including patients with acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear-positive sputum, people living with HIV (PLHIV) on antiretroviral therapy (ART), and HIV-negative patients. However, differences in treatment outcomes between shorter and longer regimens were not significant for HIV-negative individuals, except for loss to follow-up, which favored the intervention. The shorter all-oral regimen performed better across all outcomes and subgroups compared to longer regimens without new drugs. For the 2022 assessment, 8,653 records of MDR/RR-TB patients initiating treatment in 2017 were considered. Of these, 4,244 patients were treated with a shorter regimen including linezolid (used in South Africa in 2019), 880 patients received a shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing nine-month regimen with ethionamide (used in South Africa in 2017), and 850 patients were treated with longer regimens including bedaquiline and linezolid. Adverse events were noted in 5% of participants receiving the nine-month regimen with linezolid, but no comparative data were available for the ethionamide regimen. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) judged the benefits of the nine-month regimen with linezolid to be small and the undesirable effects to be moderate compared to the ethionamide regimen. The certainty of evidence was rated as very low. Based on this, the GDG concluded that the balance of health effects does not favor either regimen. Both regimens are suggested for people with pulmonary MDR/RR-TB without fluoroquinolone resistance, as a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. The cost of component medicines for both regimens was found to be similar, as both regimens have the same duration and use the same medicines except for one—linezolid instead of ethionamide. The duration of linezolid use is two months compared to four months for ethionamide, with negligible cost differences. Health care costs are also likely to be similar. The GDG noted the lack of data on the cost of managing potential long-term consequences of neurotoxicity caused by linezolid, which is a greater risk with prolonged use. The GDG emphasized that the evidence on both the intervention and comparator regimens was derived from programmatic data in South Africa, making the population and health care context comparable. However, differences between the two cohorts made it difficult to draw conclusions with full confidence. The GDG also noted the lack of systematic data collection on adverse events for the ethionamide regimen, which limited direct comparisons. The GDG acknowledged that the STREAM Stage 2 trial, a large-scale, multicountry Phase 3 trial examining a shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen, will provide additional insights into the efficacy and safety of this regimen and may increase the certainty of the evidence. The panel also considered the acceptability of the regimens, noting no significant differences in acceptability between the nine-month regimens with linezolid and ethionamide, given their overall similarity.
